It requires at least the passing of one complete generation for a bad cultural habit to die off, and this only if the next generation takes a stand against the bad cultural habit.

If no one says or does anything against the bad cultural habit, the behavior will continue on for the next generation, and the next.

Concerning social change - often it must first occur on a local level - for example, consider Burriram Province in Thailand.

In the south of the province, the district of the bicycle pagoda, every home has a large local government issued plastic barrel street side for placing their rubbish.  Likewise, there are trucks that come to collect  the garbage on a regular basis.  Hence there are no garbage fires (stinking toxic plastic and styro-foam burning) and the air is fresh and clean.  One must assume the people are both mentally and physically healthier.

But, to the north of this same province, there are no plastic barrels, no refuse pick-up, and stinking, toxic garbage fires at seemingly every home.  The air quality is horrible, even though this is the countryside and not an urban area.

Same province, different district - one group of people are awake, aware, and healthier in all respects, and the other group of people are living as if it were 100 years ago.

Why? It is not because of lack of money - same province, and both districts appear to be prospering.

It is because of local leadership - one group of leaders being awake and aware to serve the pubic interest, while another group of local leaders asleep and most probably serving their own self-interest.

So cultural change often begins at a local level, which is not to say a great effort should not be made at a national level either.

Both local and national politics should work together for the good health and welfare of the people they serve.

This again is in the Theraveda  tradition of the Thai Forest Monk.

Wat Pa Sukha To is a secluded forest meditation training and retreat center.

I can only estimate there to be 50 - 60 monks in residence, as well as about 20 - 30 nuns.

There are hundreds of lay people - day visitors and over-night visitors.
Breakfast gathering this morning seemed  to have 400 people in attendance.
There  are scores of small cabins spread about the forest (see Google Satellite map image for aerial overview) where overnight meditation practitioners stay.

All are very welcoming to me, the foreigner, and several speak English.

The amount and variety of foods at meals is overwhelming, but I will only eat once a day in the morning which is the tradition.

Here I have been able to rest after two weeks of travel - a much needed break.

Climbing the mountain (500 meters) to get here was indeed a solitary personal challenge.

My experience is that productivity is decreased while nomadic and on the road, even with tablet & 4G connectivity.

For example, we are still actively trading in crypto-currencies, but it is difficult for me to give focus and to analyze the numbers.

I have concluded that my 4G tablet with GPS is not a good enough solution for on the road connectivity, and it does not serve adequately as a camera either.

Mapping & GPS are excellent, and telegram is the best app for keeping in touch and private blogging.

Next tour I will have a different connectivety and productivity solution.

Basically I am considering a MacAirBook Clone running Linux, and a small Android phone for 4G wifi access, plus, an actual camera instead of these build in cameras.

The small Android phone must have GPS.

And, you need a separate USB power pack with solar charger.  These are very good, small and affordable these days.

In addition, on screen keyboards are a real pain. The MacAirBook clone running a full Linux system seems in my mind to be the best option.

The small Android phone adds 4G wifi access and GPS, along with quick sharing of snapshots.

Twenty and thirty years ago this land was occupied by the Thai army as it held back Khmer Rouge forces.  The Ban Kruat area is actually a Khmer resettlement area.

There are still signs of bunkers and guard shelters, but the military is long gone.

The fact that this was once a war zone is one reason it is presently ignored - too close to Cambodia ...
But from my observations, it's a great area to invest for the long term.

Buddhist monks and nuns traditionally reflect on moderation before each meal by reciting this reflection:
 
"Wisely reflecting, we take alms food, not for the purpose of fun, not for indulgence or the fascination of taste, but simply for the maintenance of the body, for the continuance of existence, for the cessation of painful feeling, for living the higher life. Through this eating, we subdue old painful feelings of hunger and prevent new painful feelings (of overeating) from arising. Thus do we live unhindered, blameless, and in comfort."
